extracted.intended_audience: general public and readers interested in U.S. Supreme Court/administrative law (law students, practitioners, policymakers)
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia-style encyclopedic summary of the Supreme Court's decision in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo (and companion Relentless), describing holdings, prior precedent, legal doctrines, background, lower-court history, opinions, and reactions. Useful as a primer on the case and its administrative-law implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chevron deference (two-step test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts defer to an agency's interpretation of an ambiguous statute if (1) the statute is ambiguous as to the specific question, and (2) the agency's interpretation is reasonable or permissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originally articulated in Chevron U.S.A., Inc. v. NRDC (1984). Step one asks whether Congress unambiguously resolved the question; if so, the court must follow Congress. If not, step two asks whether the agency's reading is reasonable; if so, courts defer to the agency. The Wikipedia article summarizes the two-step structure and its historical prevalence (cited usage in lower courts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Overruling Chevron / courts' independent judgment under the APA
rubrics_metrics.description: The Administrative Procedure Act requires courts to exercise their independent judgment in deciding whether an agency has acted within statutory authority; courts may not defer to an agency interpretation merely because a statute is ambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loper Bright holds Chevron overruled and instructs courts to decide meaning of law themselves; the decision preserves existing rules decided under Chevron but removes Chevron as a general doctrine. The majority frames this as consistent with the APA's allocation of interpretive responsibility to courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skidmore deference (persuasive-weight standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency interpretations may be given respect by courts to the extent they are persuasive, under the Skidmore framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skidmore v. Swift (1944) provides a weaker form of respect than Chevron: courts may consider agency expertise and persuasiveness but retain ultimate interpretive authority. The article states Loper Bright leaves room for Skidmore-style respect for agency views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major questions doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts require clear congressional authorization before allowing agencies to decide questions of vast economic or political significance; an agency cannot rely on ambiguous statutory language to assume such major powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited in the article via West Virginia v. EPA (2022) as a device to question administrative authority where financial/major policy consequences are at stake; used as part of the broader critique of agency interpretive reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitrary and capricious (State Farm) review
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial review of agency action for reasoned decisionmaking: a rule or action can be invalidated if it is arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referenced via administrative-law topics (State Farm standard). This is a separate ground of review from deference doctrines, focusing on whether agencies followed required procedures and made reasoned choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auer deference
rubrics_metrics.description: Deference to an agency's interpretation of its own ambiguous regulations (also known as Seminole Rock/Auer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioned in the related-topics list; historically treated as a distinct deference doctrine (interpretation of agency regulations rather than statutes). The article lists Auer among administrative-law doctrines that interact with Chevron-era jurisprudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of proposed rulemaking / notice-and-comment rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: When agencies engage in rulemaking, they generally must publish a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking and provide an opportunity for public comment (the notice-and-comment process).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article lists 'Rulemaking' and 'Notice of proposed rulemaking' among administrative-law concepts; while not elaborated in depth on this page, these are procedural requirements under the APA tied to legitimacy and reviewability of agency rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative Procedure Act (APA) responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA establishes the basic procedural framework for agency rulemaking and adjudication and governs judicial review of agency action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The majority in Loper Bright grounds its holding in the APA, emphasizing courts' interpretive duties under that statute. The article lists the APA as the statutory framework central to administrative-law review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewability doctrines (standing, ripeness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctrines like standing (Lujan) and ripeness determine whether a party has access to judicial review of agency action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article references standing (Lujan) and ripeness concepts as related topics that shape who may challenge agency rules and when; these procedural gates affect the availability and scope of review independent of deference doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nationwide injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice and doctrine governing when courts can issue injunctions that bind parties nationwide in challenges to agency action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed among related topics; the article notes nationwide injunctions as part of the litigation consequences and remedies ecosystem interacting with major administrative decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of powers and nondelegation concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Limits on Congress's delegation of legislative power to agencies and concerns about encroachment between branches shape the permissibility of agency interpretive authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concerns about separation of powers underlie parts of the opinions (e.g., Justice Thomas's concurrence arguing Chevron conflicted with separation of powers). Nondelegation doctrine and appointments issues are listed as related structural constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory authorization / organic statute requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must act within authority granted by their organic statutes; courts assess whether the statute authorizes specific agency rules or requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Loper Bright the majority found the Magnuson–Stevens Act did not authorize industry-funded monitoring; the article repeatedly emphasizes that agency rules must be grounded in clear statutory authorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhaustion of administrative remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirements that parties pursue available administrative channels before bringing certain claims to court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed in related topics (Exhaustion); this procedural requirement can affect whether and how courts review agency action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost–benefit analysis (Executive Order 12866) and consideration of implementation costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory review often involves consideration of the costs and benefits of agency rules; courts and prior opinions have criticized agencies for failing to account for implementation costs where relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited via Executive Order 12866 and West Virginia v. EPA discussion — the Court has criticized agency rules for not considering costs, which can factor into judicial review and doctrinal limits on agency action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stare decisis and treatment of prior Chevron-based decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: How precedent should be treated when a foundational doctrine is overturned; whether past agency actions decided under Chevron remain valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The majority stated that existing rules and case law decided under Chevron would remain in place, and that stare decisis does not save Chevron itself; the article discusses this tension and how prior reliance is to be handled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonableness as a metric for agency interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency's interpretation is assessed for whether it is reasonable/permissible under the statute (historically Chevron step two).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article describes 'reasonability' as the measure applied under Chevron's second step and notes lower courts used reasonableness when upholding NMFS's interpretation of statutory silence regarding monitoring costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of prior agency practice and expertise in judicial assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may consider an agency's prior practices, expertise, and persuasive reasoning when assessing the weight to give agency interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rationale underpins Skidmore and the general practice of giving some respect to agency expertise even where Chevron no longer applies; the article cites commentators who discuss recreating deference under different labels based on such factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major-impact/financial-significance scrutiny (examples: student loans, EPA regulations)
rubrics_metrics.description: When agency action has substantial financial or policy impact, courts scrutinize whether statutory text clearly authorizes such agency power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article references Biden v. Nebraska (student loan forgiveness) and West Virginia v. EPA as illustrations of courts applying heightened scrutiny where large-scale consequences are implicated, related to the major questions doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural posture and remedies (statute of limitations, Corner Post interaction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural rules like statutes of limitations and litigation devices (e.g., Corner Post decision) affect the scope and timing of re-litigation of regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes commentary that Corner Post, Inc. v. Board of Governors of the FRB could amplify re-litigation of Chevron-era regulations by creating a workaround for the six-year limitations period, showing how procedural doctrines interact with substantive review.
